W: Thanks for giving up your lunch, Emil. So, everyone's talking about the time capsule. How did you find it?
M: Honestly, it was luck. I was looking through old yearbooks in the library for my history project, and in the one from nineteen ninety-nine there's a photo of some students burying a metal box.
W: And the photo didn't say where?
M: The caption just said behind the old gym. But the old gym was knocked down years ago, so that didn't help much.
W: Then how did you work out the spot?
M: There's a huge oak tree in the background of the photo, with one branch that bends right down. That tree's still standing next to the bike shed. So I lined up the photo with the tree, and I was pretty sure the box was under the shed.
W: That's really clever. Who did the digging?
M: The caretaker did most of it. We started straight after the last bell, at half past three. He had to move two bikes and a pile of bricks first. When the shovel finally hit metal, it was half past five, and he'd missed his bus home.
W: Oh no. So what's the box like?
M: Smaller than I expected, about the size of a shoebox. It's rusty along one side, though, so I'm worried rainwater got in and spoiled some of the papers.
W: Okay. Now, about the article itself.
M: Actually, I was going to ask. Could you hold it until after the box is opened? Then you could write about what's inside and have photos of everything.
W: When's it being opened?
M: At the spring concert, in three weeks. The head teacher wants to do it on stage.
W: I see why you'd want to wait. But I've got another idea. What if we run a short story this Friday and ask anyone from the class of nineteen ninety-nine to come to the concert? The people who buried it could explain the things inside.
M: Hmm. But some of them must live far away by now.
W: Some, maybe. But lots of parents here went to this school. Somebody will know somebody. And after the concert, I'll write a second, longer piece with the photos.
M: Okay, that's actually better than my plan. Two articles, then.
W: Great. Thanks, Emil. I'll show you the first one before it goes in.

speakers.M: a school staff member who is not a teacher (for example the librarian, the nurse, the office secretary, a lab technician)

transcript:
M: Hi, come on in. You're the one who emailed about borrowing a rain gauge?
W: Yes, that's me. It's for my science fair project. I want to measure how much rain falls at school every day for five weeks.
M: Five weeks, okay. We've got two gauges in the cupboard, and the plastic one's easier to read. Where were you planning to put it?
W: I thought about the roof first, because nothing's in the way up there.
M: Students can't go on the roof, I'm afraid. It's a safety rule. But here's an idea. Put it on the ledge outside this window. You could check it without even going outside.
W: That would be easy. But I read that a gauge shouldn't sit right next to a wall. The building would block some of the rain, especially when it's windy.
M: Hmm, that's true. And this window faces away from most of our storms. So where else?
W: The vegetable garden behind the gym. It's open, there aren't any trees near it, and there's an old fence post in the corner I could tie it to.
M: The garden? I'm worried about the sprinklers. If they spray the gauge even once, your number for that day is useless.
W: I asked the garden club yesterday. They stopped using the sprinklers last month. Now they water by hand, and they said they'll stay away from that corner.
M: Well, you've really done your homework. All right, the garden it is. How often will you read it?
W: Every morning at about a quarter to eight, before the first bell. I'll write the number in my notebook and then empty it.
M: Good. And if there's a freezing night, bring it inside, because ice can crack the plastic.
W: Got it. Can I take it today?
M: Sure. Just sign this form, and bring it back to me when your five weeks are over.

author: v2-F
setting: at a small shop or cafe before opening

speakers.W: a teenager with a weekend job

transcript:
M: Morning. Before we open, have a look at this. It's the list of what we threw away last Sunday.
W: Wow. Eleven croissants and six muffins? That's a lot.
M: It is. That's about thirty dollars in the bin, and it's like that most Sundays.
W: I've been thinking about that, actually. What if we sold everything at half price after three o'clock?
M: I thought about that too. But the bakery across the road tried it last spring. The owner told me people stopped coming in the morning. They just waited for the cheap prices.
W: Oh. I didn't know that.
M: So my idea is simpler. We bake less. Twenty croissants a day instead of thirty.
W: The thing is, on Saturdays we already run out. I've been writing down when the last croissant goes, and for the past three Saturdays it's been before eleven.
M: Really? Before eleven?
W: Yeah. And people who come in for lunch get pretty annoyed when there's nothing left. Last week a man asked me twice if we had any hidden in the back.
M: Hmm. So Sundays need fewer and Saturdays need more.
W: Could the baker just make more when we're running low?
M: Only if she knows in time. She can't keep coming out of the kitchen to check the shelf.
W: I could tell her. I'm right here at the counter anyway.
M: Okay. Then twenty to start with, and you tell her when we're down to the last five. She needs about half an hour to bake a new tray.
W: That's fine. I'll keep writing down the times, too, so we can see if it's working.
M: Great. Let's start today. I'll go and tell her now, so she can get some extra dough ready. Could you put the chairs out front? We open in fifteen minutes.
W: Sure, I'll do it right away.

author: v2-H
setting: at the side of a school sports field after practice
transcript:
W: Coach, have you got a minute? It's about our starts.
M: Sure. You looked quick today. What's up?
W: Well, everyone keeps telling me I stand up too early out of the blocks, but I honestly can't feel it. I was wondering if we could film the starts and watch them back in slow motion.
M: Hmm. You know I don't allow phones at practice anymore.
W: I know. Because of last spring?
M: Right. I let everyone keep their phones on the bench, and by the end of the first week, half the team was filming silly dance videos during warm-up. Nobody stretched properly, and two runners pulled muscles.
W: But this wouldn't be phones. The library lends tablets to clubs for free. I'd borrow one, put it on a stand behind the blocks, and nobody else would touch it.
M: And then what? Everyone crowds round a screen for twenty minutes?
W: No, the replay's ready in a few seconds. Each runner watches their own start once, then goes back to the line.
M: Okay, a few seconds is fine. And I'll be honest, slow motion would help me too. At a start, feet move faster than my eyes can follow. I'm mostly guessing who pushes off badly.
W: So you'd let us do it?
M: There's one more problem. Some parents don't want their kids filmed at all. I can't just start recording.
W: What if the videos stay on the tablet and get deleted after every practice? Nothing goes online.
M: That helps. But the parents still have to agree first. I'll send a letter home with everyone this Friday, and if they all sign it, we can begin the week after.
W: So not tomorrow, then.
M: Not tomorrow. And you're in charge of the tablet. If I see it used for anything else, it goes straight back to the library.
W: Deal. I'll pick it up from the library on Monday.
M: Good. And practise keeping your head down for your first three steps. Video or no video.
